title: The robe gift
hookLine: Mahapajapati offers a robe she made; the kinds of offering

lines: SPUN AND WOVEN BY HER OWN HANDS.
THE BUDDHA SAYS: GIVE IT TO THE SANGHA.
cards: A sweater someone knitted for you. It took them weeks. It's a little lopsided, and you'd never give it away.
The hundred and forty-second discourse begins with a gift like that. The Buddha is back among the Sakyans, at Kapilavatthu.
Mahapajapati Gotami, his mother's sister, the woman who raised him after his mother died, comes to him with a new robe cloth. She spun the thread herself. She wove it herself.
This is for you, Lord, she says. Please accept it out of compassion. And the Buddha says no.

teach.b: Give it to the community, Gotami, he says. When you give to the community, both I and the community are honored. She asks again.
He says the same. A third time.
Then Ananda steps in, gently. Lord, please accept it. She was so helpful to you: your mother's sister, your nurse, your foster mother.
When your mother died, she gave you her own milk. And the Buddha has helped her too, Ananda adds: through him she found refuge and the precepts.
The Buddha agrees that each has helped the other, and that such debts can't be easily repaid with robes or food. Then he turns the moment into a teaching about giving.

He lists fourteen kinds of personal gifts, from a gift to a Buddha down to a gift to an animal. Even a gift to an animal, he says, can be expected to repay a hundredfold. Then seven kinds of gifts to the community.

teach.h: A GIFT MADE TO REACH FAR
teach.b: And four ways a gift is made pure: by the giver, by the receiver, by both, or by neither, depending on whose conduct is good. Why refuse his foster mother?

The discourse doesn't explain in a single line, and it doesn't say what happened to the robe. One common reading: he wanted her gift to reach as many people as it could, and to grow her merit beyond one person.
A later commentary tells its own story of where the robe went.
What's clear is the gift itself: thread spun by hand, for someone loved, and a teaching about generosity that grew from it.

how: In Theravada countries the Kathina ceremony at the end of the rains retreat is a major occasion when lay people offer robe cloth to the monastic community as a whole, rather than to one monk.

o: a debt that must be repaid in full
a robe worn only by senior monks
an offering, a gift given with respect

games.q: the robe gift: tap the pairs.
p: spun and wove the robe herself
she was your nurse and foster mother

s: the Buddha accepts the robe the first time it's offered
three times he asks her to give it to the community instead.

games.q: you're the Buddha. your foster mother offers you a robe she made with her own hands. what do you say, in MN 142?
o: give it to the community, and both I and they will be honored.
I can't accept gifts from family.
games.why: he asks her to give it to the whole community. Ananda pleads for her, and the Buddha teaches on the kinds of gifts.

practice: Think of someone you could give a small thing made by your own hands: a note written out, not typed; a meal; a drawing; a repaired thing.
Picture making it, and notice the care that goes in before anyone receives it, because that's part of the gift too. Then rest with the breath, and if you like, let the idea grow into a plan.

wordCard.voice: Dakkhina. An offering, a gift given with respect: Mahapajapati's handmade robe, which the Buddha asked her to give to the whole community, and the teaching on giving that followed. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali dakkhina: an offering, a gift given with respect. MN 142 is the exposition of offerings.

carryVoice: Your line: made by hand. Thread spun for one person became a teaching on giving for everyone. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 142, Dakkhinavibhanga Sutta (the exposition of offerings)
